articles.title: Dual-basket or countertop oven? The 8-quart question nobody answers
articles.standfirst: Two 3-quart drawers and one 26-quart cavity solve opposite problems. Here is the documented difference, and the one measurement that decides it for your kitchen.
articles.target_query: dual basket vs air fryer oven

sections.h: The two machines are not competing for the same job
paras: A dual-basket air fryer is one appliance pretending to be two. The Chefman 6 Qt splits a {{6 Qt / 5.67 L}} cavity into {{Two 3-quart baskets::two 3-quart baskets}} and gives each its own time and temperature, then adds Sync Finish so the shorter cook is delayed to land with the longer one.

A countertop oven is a different shape of compromise: one big cavity, many modes. The Emeril 26 QT is documented at {{26 qt / 24.6 L (manual: 1,519 cu in)}} with a dual-speed fan, a rotisserie, and French doors.

sections.h: What you can actually cook, stated in the manufacturer's own numbers
paras: The dual-basket unit's ceiling is {{450 °F / 235 °C, held for 2 minutes, for extra browning}}, over a {{200–450 °F / 95–235 °C}} range.

The oven's documented range is {{75–500 °F / 25–260 °C}} on {{120 V / 60 Hz}} at a rated {{1700 W}}. It is the only unit here that goes below 200 °F, which is what makes proofing and dehydrating possible rather than nominal.
What neither page states is how evenly either one cooks. That number does not exist on a manufacturer page, and this site does not invent it.

sections.h: The measurement that decides it
paras: Footprint, not capacity. The dual-basket unit is {{13.38 × 11.81 × 10.63 in / 33.98 × 30 × 27 cm}} and weighs {{13.3 lb / 6.03 kg}}. The oven is {{16.9 D × 15.8 W × 14.8 H in}}.
Put a tape measure on the counter and add the clearance the manual asks for behind and above the unit. A 26-quart oven that does not fit under your cabinets is not a 26-quart oven; it is a return.

sections.h: The honest summary
paras: Buy the dual-basket if you cook two things at two temperatures and want them to finish together. Buy the oven if you want one cavity that can also toast, proof and rotisserie, and you have measured the space.

If you want a single large basket instead, the third product in this set is documented as {{8 qt (brand also sells a 5 qt version of the same product page)}} and {{Designed for 4–6 people::designed for 4–6 people}} — but read that product's own page before you buy, because its Amazon listing and its brand page disagree about the temperature ceiling.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Every number above is quoted from the manufacturer's own product page or owner's manual and is linked in the source column.

articles.title: What "450 °F" actually means on an air fryer listing
articles.standfirst: On one Chefman model it is a two-minute finishing blast. On another it is a setting the manual never mentions. The badge is the same. The feature is not.

sections.h: Three different things get called "450 °F"
paras: **A full-cycle ceiling.** The Chefman 6 Qt documents a {{200–450 °F / 95–235 °C}} working range, with Hi-Fry documented as {{450 °F / 235 °C, held for 2 minutes, for extra browning}}.

**A finishing blast on a lower-ceiling unit.** Chefman's 8 Qt High Fry model is a different SKU from the stainless one this site maps: it publishes a Hi-Fry temperature of 450 °F / 232 °C and a four-function list alongside it, so the two are documented as separate things on the same page. See flag F33.

**A marketing claim with no matching manual page.** This is the case the site flags rather than resolves: the Amazon listing for the stainless 8-quart unit advertises a 450 °F Hi-Fry option, but the brand page for the model the site maps to that listing documents a {{200–400 °F}} range and four food presets.

sections.h: Why the badge matters commercially
paras: A higher ceiling is the difference between browning and steaming. But a "450 °F" badge can mean a full-cycle setting, a two-minute finish mode, or a number a copywriter typed. The only way to tell is the manual that ships with the unit — and for a listing whose model is not stated, that manual is the only document that is definitely about your machine.

sections.h: What this site does about it, and what it refuses to do
paras: It publishes both claims, side by side, with a link to each, and asserts neither. It also publishes the fact that a second Chefman 8-quart SKU exists whose documented Hi-Fry and function list match the Amazon title exactly — which makes "one of these pages is stale" the less likely explanation and "these are two different units" the more likely one.
It does not pick a winner. A fabricated resolution would be worse than a visible conflict, because you would buy on the strength of it.

sections.h: How to check in thirty seconds
paras: Open the listing. Find the model number in the product-information block. Search that exact model on the manufacturer's site. Read the specification block on that page, not the bullet points in the carousel. If the model number is absent — which it is on all three listings in this set — you are relying on the brand's word about a unit you cannot identify, and you should say so to yourself before you check out.

articles.closing_note: This explainer states no temperature for the ASIN behind product 3, because no official source states it unambiguously. That gap is published on the Flagged for review page.

articles.title: 25 presets, 24 presets, or 10-in-1? One brand page says all three
articles.standfirst: A single official product page contradicts itself four ways. That is not a scandal; it is what an unmaintained product page looks like. Here is how to read it.
articles.target_query: emeril french door air fryer 360 how many presets

sections.h: The four numbers, all from official sources
paras: On 2026-11-14 the Emeril Everyday product page for the 26 QT French Door AirFryer carried **25 Cooking Pre-sets** in its specification block, **24 one-touch cooking presets** in its description paragraph, and a feature heading reading **10-In-1 Versatility**. One of its carousel images is a file named `11-in-1_convection_oven_in_action.png`. Amazon's listing title for the same product says **24 cooking functions**.
Five official statements, four different numbers, one product.

sections.h: The manual is the tiebreaker a shopper can actually use
paras: The owner's manual linked from that same page names 24 presets for model FAFO-001, listed one by one: Airfry, Fries, Bacon, Grill, Eggs, Fish, Ribs, Defrost, Steak, Vegetables, Wings, Bake, Rotisserie, Toast, Chicken, Pizza, Pastry, Proof, Broil, Slow Cook, Roast, Dehydrate, Reheat, Warm.
That is a countable list on the document that ships with the unit, and it agrees with the description text and with Amazon. It does not agree with the page's own specification block.

sections.h: What this means for a buyer
paras: Nothing about the appliance changes when a marketing page is wrong. What changes is how much of the page you should trust. A page with four different preset counts, placeholder copy in its help section, and a carousel asset named for a feature its own heading contradicts is a page that was assembled quickly and not re-read.

The specifications that are singular and specific on that page — the dimensions, the 24.6-litre capacity and the 120-volt rating stated in that same block — are the ones to plan around, because a copy-paste error is less likely to survive in a field a shipping department needs.

sections.h: Why the site still shows no preset count for this product
paras: Because two official sources agreeing is not the same as the manufacturer publishing one number. The owner's manual names 24, so the specification row is published against the manual and not against the marketing page — and the conflict is published on the Flagged for review page so you can see exactly what was reconciled and what was not.

articles.closing_note: The manual's 24-preset list is countable and is cited to the manual. The 25, 24, 10-in-1 and 11-in-1 statements are all published verbatim on the brand's own page and are recorded on the Flagged for review page rather than smoothed over.

articles.kicker: Why this site looks like this
articles.title: Why this affiliate site shows no Amazon prices, ratings or review counts
articles.standfirst: It is not an oversight and it is not humility. Amazon's Program Policies only permit those numbers under two specific conditions, and this site meets neither.
articles.target_query: why affiliate site no amazon price

sections.h: The rule, quoted
paras: From the Associates Program Participation Requirements, section 2(b): prices and availability may be shown only if "**(a) we serve the link in which that price and availability data are displayed, or (b) you obtain Product pricing and availability data via Creators API or PA API**" and comply with the License requirements.
And from section 6(t): you may not display customer reviews or star ratings "**unless you have obtained a link to that customer review or star rating through Creators API or PA API**".

This site is a static set of pages generated from a JSON file. Amazon does not serve its links here, and there are no Creators or PA-API credentials behind it. Both conditions fail, so both categories of data are absent.

There is a third clause in the same paragraph, and it is aimed squarely at comparison pages. If you display prices for a product in any “comparison” format together with prices for the same or similar products offered through other means, “you must display both the lowest ‘new’ price and, if we provide it to you, the lowest ‘used’ price at which the Product is available on the Amazon Site”. That is why the comparison matrix on this site has no price column at all — a half-comparison is precisely what the clause is aimed at.

sections.h: The second rule people miss: no price tracking
paras: Section 6(y) is blunt: "**Unless otherwise agreed by Amazon, your Site must not have price tracking and/or price alerting functionality.**"

That rules out the most common affiliate feature of all — a price-history chart, a "price drop" alert, a "lowest ever" badge. A site that shows a price it scraped yesterday is not just out of date; it is the thing the clause is aimed at.

sections.h: What a compliant site can honestly show instead
paras: Manufacturer list prices, clearly labelled as the brand's own list price rather than a retailer price. Physical specifications, because the manufacturer owns those facts and they do not change by the hour. Commission rates from Amazon's own published table. And the gaps, named.
A number that is missing on purpose is a different object from a number that is missing by neglect. The first one a reader can trust the rest of the page around.

sections.h: The disclosure that does appear on every page
paras: Operating Agreement section 5 requires the Associate to "**clearly and prominently state**" the identification "**As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.**" — that sentence sits in the bar at the top of every page in this build, and the build fails if it is missing from any page.

The FTC's rule is the other half. A material connection must be disclosed "**clearly and conspicuously**" (16 CFR §255.5(a)), and the FTC's own guidance says the disclosure has to be placed with the endorsement rather than on a separate about page. Hence the persistent bar rather than a link in the footer.

articles.closing_note: Every quotation in this article is from a page linked in its source column and was read live. Nothing in it is legal advice; it is the rule text plus how this build implements it.

articles.title: Two 3-quart drawers or one 8-quart basket: which actually feeds four people?
articles.standfirst: The total volume is nearly identical. The cooking is not, and the difference is what you do when the first batch finishes.
articles.target_query: dual basket vs single basket air fryer

sections.h: The arithmetic, from the manufacturer's own pages
paras: The dual-basket unit is {{6 Qt / 5.67 L}} as {{Two 3-quart baskets::two 3-quart baskets}}. The single-basket unit is {{8 qt (brand also sells a 5 qt version of the same product page)}}, documented as {{Designed for 4–6 people::designed for 4–6 people}}.
So the single basket holds more at once — a third more — and the two drawers hold less per drawer but can run independently. That is the whole trade, and everything else is detail.

sections.h: What Sync Finish is actually for
paras: {{Sync Finish}} delays the start of the shorter cook so both baskets finish together; a separate Sync Baskets function copies time and temperature to the second basket.

This matters because the failure mode of batch cooking is the second batch going cold while the first one waits. A machine that plans both drawers to land at the same moment solves a problem that a bigger single basket creates rather than solves.

sections.h: Where the single basket wins
paras: One big batch of one thing. A whole chicken, a full tray of fries, a pile of wings for a crowd. Splitting 8 quarts into two 3-quart drawers means every basket-shaped item has to fit a 3-quart drawer.

The documented one-touch presets on the single-basket unit are {{Fries, Chicken, Fish, Meat (one-touch)::fries, chicken, fish, meat (one-touch)}}, and the manual publishes a default for each: {{Default 400 °F / 15 min · Meat 375 °F / 18 min · Chicken 375 °F / 22 min · Fish 350 °F / 10 min · Fries 400 °F / 20 min}}.

sections.h: The decision, stated as a decision
paras: If most of your meals are two components that should finish together, the dual basket is the better tool and the capacity number is a red herring. If most of your meals are one component in quantity, the 8-quart is the better tool and the Sync Finish feature is a feature you would never press.
This is a judgement about how people cook, not a fact from a manufacturer page, and it is labelled as such.

articles.closing_note: Neither unit was tested. Capacity, presets, defaults and features are quoted from the brand's product pages and the owner's manual for the single-basket model.

articles.title: Chefman 6 Qt Dual Basket: a review of the documents, not the machine
articles.standfirst: No unit was bought, unboxed or cooked in. What follows is a reading of Chefman's own page and manual for the TurboFry Touch 6 Qt triple-verified SKU — what it promises, what it does not, and the one number the manufacturer withholds.
articles.target_query: chefman 6 quart dual basket air fryer review

sections.h: What this review is, and what it is not
paras: This is a review of a specification sheet, and it is worth saying plainly what that means. No unit was bought, unboxed, cooked in or photographed. What follows is a reading of Chefman's own product page for the TurboFry Touch 6 Qt Dual-Window Air Fryer, model {{RJ38-SQPF-3TDB-2W}}, and its owner's manual, plus a note on what the Amazon listing says and does not say.

The FTC's guidance for endorsers is unambiguous on this point: you cannot describe an experience with a product you have not tried. So there is no "crispy fries in eight minutes" line on this page, no "we loved it", and no score out of ten. There are specifications, what they imply for a kitchen, and the gaps.

sections.h: The one-sentence version
paras: A {{6 Qt / 5.67 L}} air fryer built as {{Two 3-quart baskets::two 3-quart baskets}}, with a Sync Finish feature that times the two cooks to land together, a documented ceiling of {{200–450 °F / 95–235 °C}}, and a footprint of {{13.38 × 11.81 × 10.63 in / 33.98 × 30 × 27 cm}}.
That is the whole machine in one sentence, and it is enough to decide whether it suits your kitchen — which is the point of building the site this way.

sections.h: The temperature range is not a marketing number
paras: {{200–450 °F / 95–235 °C}} is wider at both ends than many basket fryers publish, and the low end is the interesting part: its floor is a dehydrating and proofing temperature, not a frying one. The manual is more precise about the top end than the product page is — {{450 °F / 235 °C, held for 2 minutes, for extra browning}}. Read that as a finish mode, not a full-cycle setting.

A buyer who expects a full cook cycle at the Hi-Fry temperature has read the badge, not the manual. This is the same class of problem the site documents at length for the 8-quart model, where the listing and the brand page disagree outright.

sections.h: Sync Finish is the whole product
paras: Two drawers are only better than one big basket if they are used as two drawers. The difference between a dual-basket fryer and two timers is exactly this feature: {{Yes — delays the start of the shorter cook so both baskets finish together; a separate Sync Baskets function copies time and temperature to the second basket}}.

If you would set both drawers to the same temperature for the same time anyway, you are paying for a compartment you will not use. That is not a defect in the machine; it is a mismatch with how you cook.

sections.h: The coating care line is a real constraint
paras: The owner's manual carries a specific warning about aerosol cooking sprays on the nonstick coating and recommends a non-aerosol mister instead. That is the sort of instruction people skip and then blame the pan for. It is not a defect; it is a care requirement, and Chefman documents it in the specification block itself: {{Nonstick, dishwasher-safe baskets. Manual caution: never spray with aerosol cooking oil — use a non-aerosol mister instead}}.
It matters commercially: a coating that survives year two is the difference between a repurchase and a refund, and the warranty terms are for {{1-year Chefman assurance}}.

sections.h: What Chefman does not publish
paras: Usable food volume. The 6 Qt figure is cavity volume; no usable-volume figure exists on the page or in the manual. Household size: Chefman states "designed for 4–6 people" for the 8-quart single-basket model, but the 6-quart dual-basket page makes no such claim — anyone who tells you this unit "serves four" is inferring it. An energy figure: wattage is published at {{1700 W / 120 V}}, consumption per cook is not, and it depends on how you use the machine.

And, deliberately, Amazon price, rating and review count. Amazon permits price and availability display only when it serves the link or via its official API, and customer reviews and star ratings only via the API. This site holds neither.

sections.h: The model-number caveat you should know before buying
paras: Chefman sells several very similar 6-quart dual machines. This page's model, {{RJ38-SQPF-3TDB-2W}}, is the dual-window version; the sister SKU is {{RJ38-SQPF-3TDB-2 (labelled 'Dual-Basket' on chefman.com)}}. They share a price ladder and a form factor on the brand's own site, and a later pass found a third 6-quart dual-basket SKU on the brand's site as well — see the Flagged page, F32.

The Amazon listing's title mentions easy-view windows, which corresponds to the dual-window model, but Amazon does not publish a manufacturer model number on an ASIN, so this is a documented match rather than an official cross-reference. That is why this page does not claim "the listing you clicked is exactly this model".

sections.h: Who this machine is for
paras: If your dinners routinely involve two components that want different temperatures, and the failure mode you are trying to avoid is one component going cold while the other finishes, the documented design of this unit addresses precisely that. If your dinners are usually one thing in a large batch, an 8-quart single basket gives you more usable volume per square inch of counter, and Chefman publishes one in this same set.

The specification sheet will not tell you whether the food tastes good. Nothing can, except cooking in it. What it can tell you is whether the machine's documented behaviour matches the way you cook — and on that question, the documents are unusually complete.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Every number above is quoted from the manufacturer's own product page or owner's manual and is linked in the source column.

articles.title: How to read an air fryer spec sheet: the eight lines that actually decide it
articles.standfirst: Listings are long on adjectives and short on the eight lines that determine whether a machine fits your kitchen. Walk them in this order and most of the market falls away before you look at a price.
articles.target_query: how to read air fryer specifications

sections.h: 1. Temperature range, not "max temperature"
paras: The range tells you what the machine can hold; the max tells you what it can briefly reach. The Emeril oven documents {{75–500 °F / 25–260 °C}}; the Chefman 8-quart basket documents {{200–400 °F}}; the Chefman 6-quart dual documents {{200–450 °F / 95–235 °C}}.

Read the low end too. The Emeril's floor is low enough to proof dough and dehydrate; the basket fryers start where frying starts. Neither is a defect, but only one of the three can double as a dehydrator.

sections.h: 2. Capacity — and whether it is two compartments
paras: Capacity is the most-abused number on the box because it measures cavity volume, not food. The useful question is not "how many quarts" but "how many independent compartments, and what is each one's volume". The Chefman dual-basket answers both: {{6 Qt / 5.67 L}} total, {{Two 3-quart baskets::two 3-quart baskets}}. The Emeril answers with one number: {{26 qt / 24.6 L (manual: 1,519 cu in)}}.

Two smaller drawers and one large drawer can hold similar total volume and cook very differently. The single-basket 8-quart model publishes just the total and no per-basket figure, because there is no second basket.

sections.h: 3. Footprint, and the clearance nobody mentions
paras: Measure your counter, then measure the gap to the cabinet above it. The Chefman 6 Qt dual is {{13.38 × 11.81 × 10.63 in / 33.98 × 30 × 27 cm}}; the Chefman 8 Qt is {{8 Qt model: 15.4 × 12.6 × 13.5 in / 39.11 × 32 × 34.29 cm · 12.8 lb / 5.8 kg}}; the Emeril is {{16.9 D × 15.8 W × 14.8 H in}}.

The Emeril manual goes further than any of them and specifies free space on top, back and sides, and never under a hanging cabinet. For an oven-style unit of that height, the clearance requirement is a real constraint on where the machine can live — not a footnote.

sections.h: 4. Weight, because you will lift it
paras: A machine you cannot comfortably lift is a machine you will not clean properly. Chefman publishes {{13.3 lb / 6.03 kg}} for the 6-quart dual and {{8 Qt model: 15.4 × 12.6 × 13.5 in / 39.11 × 32 × 34.29 cm · 12.8 lb / 5.8 kg}} for the 8-quart.
The Emeril brand page publishes dimensions but not weight. That is a genuine gap in the spec sheet, and it is listed as such on the Flagged page rather than filled in from a retailer listing.

sections.h: 5. Wattage and the circuit it sits on
paras: All three machines draw serious power. Chefman publishes {{1700 W / 120 V}} for both basket models; the Emeril manual gives {{1700 W}} at {{120 V / 60 Hz}}.

If you plan to run one of these on the same circuit as a kettle or a coffee machine, that is the line to check against your breaker panel. This site does not give electrical advice beyond quoting the manufacturer's rating.

sections.h: 6. What is dishwasher-safe, and what the manual forbids
paras: "Dishwasher-safe" almost always means specific parts, not the whole machine. Chefman says the 8-quart basket and rack are top-rack dishwasher-safe, and its manuals warn specifically against aerosol cooking sprays on the nonstick coating.
That warning is worth more than any feature bullet, because it determines whether the coating survives year two.

sections.h: 7. Presets — count them only if the manufacturer does
paras: Preset counts are where spec sheets go to die. The Chefman 8-quart page lists {{Fries, Chicken, Fish, Meat (one-touch)::fries, chicken, fish, meat (one-touch)}} and its manual gives the default time and temperature for each. The Emeril brand page, by contrast, states its count several different ways on the same page, and the Amazon listing states it again differently. That is why no preset count is asserted for the Emeril anywhere on this site; the manual's individually named presets are the only countable set.
There is a whole article on that single discrepancy, because it is the clearest example on this site of why "the official page says so" is not the same as "the official page is consistent".

sections.h: 8. Warranty, and what it excludes
paras: Chefman publishes a {{Limited 1-year warranty from date of retail purchase (non-transferable, original purchaser)::limited 1-year warranty from date of retail purchase (non-transferable, original purchaser)}} in the 8-quart manual and {{1-year Chefman assurance}} on both basket product pages. The Emeril page publishes {{1-year warranty}}.
Read the terms document, not the badge — a warranty that excludes the coating is not covering the part that fails.

sections.h: The line that is not on the spec sheet at all
paras: Price and customer rating. This site does not publish either for an Amazon listing, because Amazon's Program Policies permit price and availability display only when Amazon serves the link or via its official API, and customer reviews and star ratings only via that API. Manufacturer list prices are published here in a separate, clearly labelled column with their own sources, because those are the brand's own numbers, not Amazon's.

A five-minute version: write down the width of the gap above your counter; write down how many people you cook for on a normal night; decide whether you need two compartments or one cavity; find the owner's manual PDF and read the temperature range and preset chart; only then look at price on the retailer, where it is current.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Every number above is quoted from the manufacturer's own product page or owner's manual and is linked in the source column.

articles.title: 26 quarts, 1,519 cubic inches: an honest air fryer capacity guide
articles.standfirst: Quart capacity is a cavity measurement, not a food measurement. So this guide uses the numbers the manufacturers print, shows the arithmetic they imply, and is explicit about the one thing none of them publishes: usable food volume.

sections.h: What the brands actually publish
paras: Three units, three different ways of stating the same idea, all from official pages. The dual-window fryer is {{6 Qt / 5.67 L}}. The single-basket fryer is sold in two sizes on one page, listed as {{8 qt (brand also sells a 5 qt version of the same product page)}}. The countertop oven is {{26 qt / 24.6 L (manual: 1,519 cu in)}}.
The oven is the only one that publishes a cubic-inch figure as well as a litre figure, which lets you check the arithmetic instead of taking it on trust.

sections.h: Do the arithmetic, because the brands make you
paras: The oven's owner's manual gives its specification table as model FAFO-001, 120 V/1700 W/60 Hz, rated power 1700 W, capacity 26 quarts (1,519 cubic inches), 75 °F - 500 °F, LED display. Converting 1,519 cubic inches gives roughly **24.9 litres**. The brand's own page states {{26 qt / 24.6 L (manual: 1,519 cu in)}}.

Those two figures sit about one per cent apart — close enough that both describe the same cavity, and far enough apart that anyone quoting litres to two decimal places should say which document it came from. The two Chefman figures need no conversion at all: they are printed on the brand's own specification blocks.
**The conversion is arithmetic, not a published figure.** The published numbers are 26 quarts and 24.6 litres. Where this site shows a derived number, it says so.

sections.h: The only household-size claim in this set — and why it is the only one
paras: Exactly one official page in this product set maps a capacity to a number of people: the single-basket fryer is {{Designed for 4–6 people::designed for 4–6 people}}. No other unit here makes that mapping, and the oven's page, which does describe the cavity as spacious, stops short of assigning it to a family size.

That single claim is worth more than a page of folk maths, because it is a manufacturer telling you how it expects the product to be used. Everything else — the “feeds 6-8”, “perfect for a family of four” lines that fill comparison blogs — is somebody's estimate built on a quart figure that was never a food volume to begin with.

One caution on that page: it covers two products, the 5 qt and the 8 qt, and the capacity, dimensions and weight rows are given for both. Check which model you are reading before you measure your shelf.

sections.h: What nobody publishes: usable food volume
paras: This is the number that would actually answer “will this feed my family”, and not one of these three manufacturers publishes it. Usable volume is smaller than cavity volume because the heating element, the basket walls and the rack all take space, and how much depends on the food.

So this guide cannot tell you how many chicken wings fit, and neither can any other page that quotes only a quart figure. What it can tell you is the relative scale, which is a real decision. The 8 qt is a single cavity of 7.57 L that the brand says is designed for 4–6 people. The 6 qt is the same class of cooking in two 3-quart baskets — the same nominal total, split so two dishes can finish together. The 26 qt is a different category entirely, documented with a rotisserie, a crisper tray, a baking pan and a wire rack.
Any page that tells you the exact number of drumsticks will be guessing. This one will not.

sections.h: Before you measure your counter
paras: Capacity is the number you will argue about with other shoppers. Counter space is the number that will argue with your kitchen. The oven's manual sets out its own ventilation requirements: leave at least 5 inches of free space on the top, back and sides, never put anything on top of the appliance, and never operate it under hanging cabinets. The unit measures {{16.9 D × 15.8 W × 14.8 H in}}.

The fryers need less: {{13.38 × 11.81 × 10.63 in / 33.98 × 30 × 27 cm}} for the dual-window unit, and {{8 Qt model: 15.4 × 12.6 × 13.5 in / 39.11 × 32 × 34.29 cm · 12.8 lb / 5.8 kg}} for the single-basket one.
And if you are still choosing between them, the form-factor question comes before capacity, and the toaster-oven question comes before both.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this set publishes a usable food volume, and none has been tested by anyone who wrote this. Those gaps are real, and they are why this site refuses to declare a winner.

articles.title: Will it actually fit? Three air fryers, measured against your counter
articles.standfirst: Every manufacturer on this site publishes outer dimensions. That turns 'will it fit' from a guess into arithmetic — and it is the one buying question a spec sheet can answer completely.

sections.h: The number you measure first is not the width
paras: Most counter-space failures are depth or height failures, because people measure the width of the gap they can see and ignore the distance the appliance needs in front of it. The Emeril is documented at {{16.9 D × 15.8 W × 14.8 H in}}, and its French doors swing forward rather than up, so the space in front of it matters as much as the space under the cabinet.

The two Chefman units are both shorter and shallower on paper. The dual-window 6 Qt is documented at {{13.38 × 11.81 × 10.63 in / 33.98 × 30 × 27 cm}}. The 8 Qt's published row reads {{8 Qt model: 15.4 × 12.6 × 13.5 in / 39.11 × 32 × 34.29 cm · 12.8 lb / 5.8 kg}}. Read the manual's own clearance instructions before deciding — a published outer dimension is not a published clearance.

sections.h: Weight matters when you lift it out to clean
paras: These are not built-in appliances. Every one of them gets lifted, wiped and put back, so weight is a daily detail rather than a shipping detail. The manufacturer's own figure for the 6 Qt dual-window is {{13.3 lb / 6.03 kg}}. The 8 Qt publishes its weight on the same line as its dimensions — {{8 Qt model: 15.4 × 12.6 × 13.5 in / 39.11 × 32 × 34.29 cm · 12.8 lb / 5.8 kg}} — and the Emeril's specification block does not state a weight.
If the appliance is going above shoulder height or into a cupboard, that is the number to weigh, not the capacity.

sections.h: Capacity per square inch of counter
paras: The interesting ratio is how much cooking volume each unit buys per unit of counter it occupies. The 6 Qt dual-window gives {{Two 3-quart baskets::two 3-quart baskets}} inside a footprint of roughly 158 square inches. The 8 Qt single basket gives {{8 qt (brand also sells a 5 qt version of the same product page)}} on a slightly larger footprint. The Emeril gives {{26 qt / 24.6 L (manual: 1,519 cu in)}} on the largest footprint of the three.

That ratio is arithmetic on published numbers, not a measurement of usable volume: a manufacturer's quart figure and a usable cooking area are not the same thing, and no official source read for this site states usable interior area.

sections.h: What this page cannot tell you
paras: It cannot tell you the clearance your cabinet manufacturer requires, the heat your countertop tolerates, or how loud the fan is — none of that is published by these brands in the pages read for this site. Measure the gap, read the manual's clearance section, and treat the published outer dimensions as the starting point rather than the answer.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Every dimension is quoted from the manufacturer's own product page or owner's manual and is linked per section.

articles.title: Who pays for the air-fryer review you are reading?
articles.standfirst: Affiliate links are not a scandal and they are not invisible. Here is exactly how this site earns, what Amazon requires it to say, and the three claims it is not allowed to make.

sections.h: The disclosure is a contract term, not a courtesy
paras: Amazon's own guidance is precise about the wording: the Operating Agreement requires that the statement “As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.” clearly and conspicuously appears on the site. That is why the sentence sits above the header on every page here rather than in a footer nobody scrolls to.

The same page adds the link-level rule: the disclosure next to a link must be **clear** — examples given are '(paid link)', '#ad' or '#CommissionsEarned' — and **conspicuous**, placed near the link rather than somewhere a reader has to hunt for it.

sections.h: US law adds a second, independent requirement
paras: The FTC's influencer guidance says to disclose any financial relationship with a brand, to place the disclosure so it is hard to miss, and to use simple language. It also states plainly that the disclosure should sit with the endorsement itself, not only on a profile page or at the end of a post.
The binding rule behind that guidance is 16 CFR Part 255, whose §255.5 is titled 'Disclosure of material connections'.

sections.h: The three claims an affiliate site may not make
paras: First, it may not claim hands-on experience it does not have — the FTC's own line is that you cannot talk about your experience with a product you have not tried. Every article on this site therefore states that nothing was tested.

Second, it may not publish Amazon prices, availability, star ratings or customer reviews unless Amazon serves the content or it comes through the official API. That is why every price on this site is either a manufacturer's own list price or blank.
Third, it may not run price-tracking or price-alert functionality unless Amazon agrees to it. A build check in this repository fails the build if such a component is added.

sections.h: What that leaves for a site like this one
paras: It leaves documentation. Capacity, dimensions, temperature ranges, basket counts, door types and warranty terms are all published by the manufacturer, all verifiable by a reader in two clicks, and none of them require the author to have switched the appliance on.
That is a narrower promise than most affiliate sites make, and it is the only one that can be kept without testing.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Policy quotations link to the Amazon, FTC and eCFR pages they were read from.

articles.title: The 1,700-watt question: what an air fryer actually asks of your kitchen
articles.standfirst: All three units are documented at 1,700 watts on 120 volts. That number decides more than browning — it decides whether the appliance can share a circuit.

sections.h: Wattage is a circuit question before it is an electricity-bill question
paras: Every one of these three appliances is documented at {{1700 W / 120 V}} or the equivalent 1,700-watt, 120-volt specification on its manufacturer page or manual. A 1,700-watt load on a 120-volt circuit draws about 14 amps, which is most of a standard 15-amp kitchen circuit.

That is why the manual, not the marketing page, is the place to look for the appliance's own instructions about not sharing the outlet. This site does not restate electrical code, because electrical code is not published by these manufacturers and this site does not publish what it cannot source.

sections.h: What the electricity actually costs
paras: Energy cost is arithmetic you can do exactly: kilowatts multiplied by hours multiplied by the price per kilowatt-hour on your own bill. The appliance's kilowatt figure is published — 1,700 W is 1.7 kW. The hours and the tariff are yours.
This site deliberately does not quote an average electricity price: no official source read for this project publishes one for a specific reader, and an average is not a bill.

sections.h: Why 'faster than the oven' is not the same as 'cheaper'
paras: A smaller cavity heats faster and loses less heat when opened, which is the documented logic behind a countertop appliance — the Chefman pages describe cooking without preheating, and the Emeril page describes a dual-speed fan and 360° circulation. But none of those pages states a comparison of kilowatt-hours against a full-size oven, and this site does not invent one.
If that comparison matters to you, it can be measured with a plug-in energy monitor in an afternoon. It cannot be established from a specification page.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested, and no electricity price is asserted. Wattage figures are quoted from the manufacturers and linked per section.

articles.title: The 8-quart Chefman is sold as two different machines — and the listing describes both
articles.standfirst: One SKU tops out at 400°F. Another reaches 450°F for the final two minutes. The supplied Amazon link's title names the feature of one and the finish of the other.
articles.target_query: chefman 8 qt air fryer model difference

sections.h: Two official pages, two temperature ceilings
paras: Chefman's own store publishes a stainless 8-quart unit with a documented temperature range of {{200–400 °F}} and four cooking presets.

On a different product page, Chefman publishes a matte-black 8-quart unit, model RJ38-8T-BLACK, with a 'Hi-Fry' button that raises the temperature to 450°F for the final two minutes and lists exactly four functions: air fry, bake, dehydrate and frozen.

sections.h: Why this is not a contradiction — it is a catalogue
paras: Two model numbers two different products. What makes it confusing is the supplied Amazon listing: its title reads 'Chefman Air Fryer 8 Qt | TurboFry 4-in-1 with 450°F Hi-Fry Option for Crispier Results | Bake, Dehydrate, Frozen | XL Nonstick Dishwasher-Safe Basket | Stainless Steel'.

The 450°F Hi-Fry and the exact function list match the black RJ38-8T-BLACK page. The finish matches the stainless page. A title can be edited independently of a SKU, and Amazon does not publish the model number in a place a search engine reliably reads, so this site does not choose between them.

sections.h: What to do with this if you are buying
paras: Open the listing and read the model number in the Product information section. If it says RJ38-8T-BLACK, expect the 450°F Hi-Fry button and four functions. If it says RJ38-SQSS-8T, expect a 400°F ceiling and four presets.
That single line resolves a question this repository has carried as an open flag through seven verification passes, because it is the one fact that only a rendered listing page shows.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Both model pages and the listing title were read on 2026-11-15 and are linked above.

articles.title: Sync Finish, explained by the manual that ships with it
articles.standfirst: One button promises two baskets that end at the same time. The owner's manual spells out exactly how that works, exactly when it breaks, and what the other sync button does instead.

sections.h: What Sync Finish does, in the manual's own words
paras: The TurboFry Touch dual-window model publishes the feature as: {{Yes — delays the start of the shorter cook so both baskets finish together; a separate Sync Baskets function copies time and temperature to the second basket}}. That is this site's condensed record; the owner's manual describes the same behaviour step by step.

To use it, both baskets are set to their own times and temperatures, the SYNC FINISH button is pressed, and the unit starts the side with the longer cook first. The manual states that it delays the start of the other side until the appropriate moment so that they finish together, and that the basket which is waiting displays HOLD on the panel until it begins.

Sync Baskets is the second button, and it does something different: it applies the time and temperature set on the first basket to the second, so both baskets cook identically rather than finish together. The manual calls it a shortcut for setting both baskets to cook simultaneously with the same time and temperature.

sections.h: How each one behaves once cooking starts
paras: Under Sync Baskets, an adjustment made to one basket while cooking is applied to the other automatically, so the two stay matched. Under Sync Finish, an adjustment made while one basket is still waiting keeps the finish synced, provided the shorter cook time is not raised above the longer one.

The pause behaviour is documented too: when either basket is pulled out during cooking, both sides pause until it is returned. The SHAKE light comes on as a reminder to shake or flip food, and goes off on its own after about a minute if the basket is not pulled out.

sections.h: What breaks the sync
paras: Two documented actions break it. Pressing the HI-FRY button — the one that raises the cooking temperature to {{450 °F / 235 °C, held for 2 minutes, for extra browning}} — lifts one basket out of the shared schedule: in the sync modes, the manual says pressing it raises the temperature only on that basket and breaks the sync. The +2 MIN button does the same.

The manual adds a detail worth knowing before a second batch: while the unit cooks on one side, the other basket can still be started later, but the SYNC BASKETS and SYNC FINISH functions will not be available for that cook.

sections.h: What this feature is not
paras: It is not a promise about doneness. Finishing at the same time is a scheduling behaviour documented by the manufacturer; whether each basket is cooked through is still a check the cook makes, and the manual's own advice is to check foods for doneness against current safety guidelines before serving.

It is also not a feature of every machine in this set. The manual for the 8 Qt TurboFry Touch — which this site also reads — lists one basket in its features section, so there is no second basket for two buttons to coordinate; the sync functions are documented only on the dual-window model's manual. That difference is recorded in the dataset as {{Not documented for RJ38-SQSS-8T on the brand page or in its manual::not documented for RJ38-SQSS-8T on the brand page or in its manual}}, on the row that asks whether a basket divider exists for the 8 Qt model.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. The sync behaviour is quoted from the owner's manual linked per section, and the feature row comes from the manufacturer's own product page.

articles.title: The aerosol-oil caution nobody reads, quoted instead of paraphrased
articles.standfirst: Chefman's dual-window manual carries one CAUTION about spray cans that decides whether a nonstick basket keeps its coating. The sentence is short enough to quote whole, so this page does.
articles.target_query: aerosol cooking oil air fryer nonstick coating

sections.h: The sentence, in the manual's own words
paras: The dual-window model's manual puts the rule inside the operating instructions, between a CAUTION marker and the step about loading food: “Never spray the baskets or racks with cooking oil from an aerosol spray can, which includes harsh components that can cause chipping of the nonstick coating. However, you can oil the racks or spray them with oil from a non-aerosol mister.”

The dataset publishes the same rule in its condensed form: {{Nonstick, dishwasher-safe baskets. Manual caution: never spray with aerosol cooking oil — use a non-aerosol mister instead}}. Both point at the same page; the manual is the primary document and is linked under this section.

sections.h: What the caution says, and what it leaves out
paras: It names a cause and an effect — aerosol spray cans, harsh components, chipping of the nonstick coating — and it offers the substitute in the same breath: oil the racks, or spray them, from a non-aerosol mister. It does not set out a general oil rule; the manual handles that separately, telling the reader to toss food with a little oil in a separate bowl rather than filling the baskets.

The cleaning section carries the rest of the care story for the same model: the baskets and racks are top-rack dishwasher safe, the unit itself is wiped with a damp cloth and never submerged, and abrasive cleansers are off the list because they can damage the finishes.

sections.h: The other model's care row, stated exactly as recorded
paras: For the 8 Qt TurboFry Touch, this site's dataset records a shorter care row: {{Nonstick basket and rack; top-rack dishwasher safe}}. No aerosol rule is recorded for that model in this dataset, and this article quotes the caution only where the dataset carries it. If the second manual ever needs the same warning quoted, the source document is linked and the row can be checked against it.

That restraint is deliberate. A care instruction softened in retelling — the caution becoming “be careful with sprays”, the rule becoming optional — stops doing its job. Quoting the manufacturer's sentence keeps the obligation exact, and it gives the reader a link to the document that wrote it.

articles.closing_note: No product in this article was tested. The quoted caution is from the manufacturer's owner's manual, and the care rows come from the dataset's verified entries for each product.

articles.title: 1700 watts, three manuals, and one extension-cord rule that is not the same
articles.standfirst: All three appliances in this set carry the same wattage rating from their manufacturers. Their manuals do not agree on how to power them, and one of the three rules is absolute.
articles.target_query: air fryer 1700 watts extension cord manual

sections.h: The same rating, three times
paras: The Chefman 6 Qt dual-window model documents {{1700 W / 120 V}} on its product page. The Chefman 8 Qt TurboFry Touch documents {{1700 W / 120 V}} on its page as well. The Emeril Lagasse French Door AirFryer 360 documents a rated power of {{1700 W}} on {{120 V / 60 Hz}}.

The Emeril's specification table in its owner's manual states the same figures for model FAFO-001, and its heating-element section attributes the turbo-fan mode to a top spiral heating element at that same wattage. Nothing in this paragraph is an estimate; each figure is a published dataset value with the manufacturer's page behind it.

sections.h: The Chefman manuals: an extension cord is allowed, with one condition
paras: Both Chefman manuals explain that the supplied cord is deliberately short, to reduce entanglement and tripping hazards. A longer detachable extension cord may be used if care is exercised, and both manuals attach the same condition: the marked electrical rating of the extension cord should be at least as great as the electrical rating of the appliance. The longer cord, they add, should be arranged so it will not drape over a countertop or tabletop where it can be pulled on or tripped over.
Before any of that, both manuals ask a question most buyers skip: check that the home power supply corresponds with the intended voltage of the appliance.

sections.h: The Emeril manual: the rule is absolute
paras: The French Door AirFryer 360's manual states it differently, in its safeguards: never use with an extension cord. That line is the manufacturer's, not this site's, and it is the sharpest single instruction in this comparison.

The same safeguards section defines where the appliance may sit: a flat, heat-resistant surface, countertop use only, not in an enclosed space or under hanging cabinets, with free space left on the top, back and sides and above the appliance, and never on a cooktop.

sections.h: What a buyer can take from three manuals
paras: If one of these appliances is heading for a kitchen where the outlet is far from the counter, the manuals' difference matters before any feature does. Two manufacturers permit a rated extension cord with care; the third forbids the cord outright and instead defines the clearance around the unit.
None of this is this site's advice. It is each manufacturer's instruction, quoted from the manuals and linked per section, with the wattage rows taken from the dataset's published values.

articles.closing_note: No appliance in this article was plugged in, measured or tested. The power rows are published dataset values sourced to the manufacturer pages, and the cord instructions are quoted from the owner's manuals.

articles.title: Seven accessories, a six-accessory title, and one honest caveat
articles.standfirst: Two of Emeril's own documents say 7 accessories. Amazon's title for the same listing says six. The owner's manual settles the count and then takes it back — here is what each document actually says.
articles.target_query: emeril lagasse french door airfryer 360 what accessories are included

sections.h: Two brand documents say seven. The Amazon title says six.
paras: The Emeril product page states, in one sentence: "Included are 7 premium accessories to maximize versatility—air fry basket, rotisserie spit, bake pan, and more."

The Amazon listing title for the same product ends with "Six Cooking Accessories Included" — one fewer than the brand's own count. The full title is quoted on the product's data page, and the disagreement is recorded in that product's flag register rather than resolved by picking a winner. This site publishes the count the two brand documents agree on.

The owner's manual takes the third, most useful approach: it enumerates thirteen numbered parts. Six are built into the appliance (main unit, door handle, glass door, LED display, control panel, control knob), which leaves {{7}} removable accessories: a drip tray, a wire rack, a baking pan, a rotisserie spit, a crisper tray, a rotisserie fetch tool and a plate handle.

sections.h: The manual's caveat is the sentence that matters
paras: Immediately after its parts list, the manual says: "Some accessories may not be included with purchase." That is the manufacturer declining to guarantee its own accessory count — and it is the one line almost no retail listing quotes.

Judgement: for a buyer who needs a specific accessory — the rotisserie spit for a recipe, the bake pan for a family meal — the count is trivia and the caveat is the fact. Check the box on delivery day; the documents give no promise to enforce.

sections.h: The Chefman documents answer a different question
paras: Neither Chefman unit publishes an accessory count at all. The 6 Qt dual-basket's care row reads: {{Nonstick, dishwasher-safe baskets. Manual caution: never spray with aerosol cooking oil — use a non-aerosol mister instead}}. Baskets and racks, described by coating and cleaning rather than by a parts list.

The 8 Qt TurboFry's documents name its removable parts as: {{Nonstick basket and rack; top-rack dishwasher safe}} — and stop there. Its brand page sells the machine around them: {{Fries, Chicken, Fish, Meat (one-touch)}} presets, an {{LED shake reminder}}, and {{Designed for 4–6 people::designed for 4–6 people}} as the household pitch.

So the honest cross-brand comparison is not seven versus nothing. It is that one manufacturer documents a box list with a caveat, and the other two publish no count anywhere this site could verify — a gap, which is left visible here rather than filled from a third-party seller's guess.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was unboxed or tested. The accessory counts come from the Emeril product page, its owner's manual and the Amazon listing title, each linked where cited.

articles.title: Rotisserie at home: what the 26 QT's manual actually documents
articles.standfirst: The preset and the spit set are in the manual. What the manual never claims — cooked weights, times, doneness — is the part worth reading before you plan a chicken dinner.
articles.target_query: emeril lagasse 26qt french door airfryer rotisserie

sections.h: What is documented
paras: The published spec row is deliberately narrow: {{Yes (manual documents a rotisserie preset and spit set)}} That wording summarizes two documents without stretching either: the brand page's feature list, which shows a Rotisserie section, and the owner's manual, whose preset chart lists Rotisserie by name and whose parts list includes the spit.

The rotisserie preset is one of the {{24 presets are named in the owner's manual for model FAFO-001: Airfry, Fries, Bacon, Grill, Eggs, Fish, Ribs, Defrost, Steak, Vegetables, Wings, Bake, Rotisserie, Toast, Chicken, Pizza, Pastry, Proof, Broil, Slow Cook, Roast, Dehydrate, Reheat, Warm}} The count itself has a history: the brand's spec block says "25 Cooking Pre-sets" while the same page's description says "24 one-touch cooking presets" — the manual is treated as the controlling document here.
The spit is one of the {{7}} removable accessories counted from the manual's parts list, and the manual immediately concedes: "Some accessories may not be included with purchase."

sections.h: The machine the spit turns inside
paras: The cavity is {{26 qt / 24.6 L (manual: 1,519 cu in)}} — the reason a whole bird is plausible on paper. The doors are {{French doors, single-pull opening::french doors, single-pull opening}}; the air system is {{Dual-speed fan, 360° air circulation::dual-speed fan, 360° air circulation}}. The oven runs on {{120 V / 60 Hz}} at {{1700 W}}, with a documented range of {{75–500 °F / 25–260 °C}}.

Numbers the documents do not publish: a maximum rotisserie weight, a suggested time per pound, a doneness temperature. None of those appears on the brand page or in the manual, so none appears here. Judgement: a recipe that needs them will come from a cookbook or a tested source, not from this spec sheet.

sections.h: The counting problem, stated plainly
paras: The same brand page markets this oven as "10-in-1" in its feature headings while listing 24–25 presets elsewhere. Two counting systems, neither defined, on one page. This site's position is boring on purpose: report the manual's named presets, ignore the marketing arithmetic, and record the disagreement in the flag register so a reader can check it.
No unit was tested for this article. Everything above is a description of documents — which is exactly as far as a documentation-based site can honestly go on a feature like rotisserie.

articles.closing_note: No unit in this article was tested. Preset names, the parts list and the accessory caveat were read from the owner's manual; the conflicting preset counts are quoted from the brand page and the Amazon title, all linked where cited.

articles.title: What 'As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases' actually obliges
articles.standfirst: The sentence in this site's header is a contract clause with a mandated wording and a placement rule. Who requires it, what it must look like, and the things it does not do.

sections.h: The sentence is a contract clause, not a courtesy
paras: Amazon's Associates Program Operating Agreement, section 5, requires it: 'You must clearly and prominently state the following … on your Site …: "As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases."' The wording inside the quotation marks is the only disclosure text the agreement mandates — a site may not invent a prettier paraphrase and call it compliant.

The agreement makes the requirement load-bearing in section 6(a): 'any violation of Section 5 and as specified in the Program Policies will be deemed a material breach of this Agreement.' Material breach is the termination clause — the difference between a style critique and losing the account.

sections.h: Where the sentence has to sit
paras: Amazon's text sets a placement standard — 'clearly and prominently' — and the FTC's guidance for endorsements fills in what that means physically: the disclosure must be 'hard to miss' and 'placed with the endorsement message itself', not parked on an About page or at the end of a post where a reader has already made up their mind.

The codified rule underneath is 16 CFR §255.5, titled 'Disclosure of material connections'. An affiliate commission is a financial material connection — the exact situation the rule addresses — so the disclosure is not optional politeness; it is the mechanism the rule prescribes.

sections.h: The things the sentence does not do
paras: It does not license untested claims. The FTC's companion rule is blunt: 'You can't talk about your experience with a product you haven't tried.' No product in this set was tested, so no article here narrates cooking results.

It does not unlock Amazon's data. Prices, availability, star ratings and review counts may be shown only when Amazon serves them or through the official API — the reason every price on this site is a manufacturer's list price or a blank cell.
It does not make the site Amazon's voice. The same section 5 forbids misrepresenting the relationship, 'including by expressing or implying that we support, sponsor, or endorse you'.
And it does not vary by page. A review, a comparison or a buying guide carries the same obligation as the homepage — the disclosure travels with the endorsement, per the FTC's placement rule.

sections.h: How this site implements it
paras: The sentence is emitted into the header of every page this site generates, above the first paragraph, and the site builder fails the build if a page ships without it. That is the practical answer to 'clearly and prominently': one fixed sentence, one fixed place, on every page, with the underlying documents linked from the compliance page.

articles.closing_note: This article explains published rules; it is not legal advice. Policy quotations were re-read from the live Amazon, FTC and eCFR pages on 2026-11-16 and link to those pages.
